claims.text: Adding approximately 10 vol% SiC to ZrB2 enables reactive densification at about 1700 °C.
SiC addition promotes in-situ formation of a protective silica-rich interfacial phase.
The silica-rich interfacial phase improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The silica-rich interfacial phase improves resistance to corrosion by liquid plating metals.
Single-phase ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C exhibits excellent high-temperature strength.
Single-phase ZrB2 is difficult to fabricate by lower-temperature processing routes.
ZrB2 processed at reduced sintering temperatures suffers from oxidation and corrosion limitations.
During service, oxidation of the SiC-derived phase produces a thin, continuous silica or silicate layer.
The silica or silicate layer acts as a diffusion barrier.
SiC accelerates mass transport through reactive liquid-phase sintering or transient-liquid formation.
Accelerated mass transport lowers the temperature required to densify ZrB2.
Silicon preferentially oxidizes to form a protective SiO2 or silicate scale at grain boundaries and interfaces.
The SiO2 or silicate scale retards oxygen ingress.
The SiO2 or silicate scale reduces attack by liquid plating metals.
ZrB2 with approximately 10 vol% SiC, processed at about 1700 °C, will have compressive strength and hardness comparable to or greater than conventional single-phase ZrB2.
The SiC-containing composite will show lower oxidation weight gain than ZrB2 fabricated near 1700 °C without a sintering aid.
The SiC-containing composite will resist liquid plating-metal corrosion better than ZrB2 fabricated near 1700 °C without a sintering aid.
The proposed benefits are expected to persist at service temperatures up to approximately 2000 °C when the silica-based scale remains stable.
Scale spallation would diminish the proposed performance benefits.
Excessive silicon concentration may disrupt cohesion of the ceramic matrix and diminish the proposed benefits.
